newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Commerzbank sees steady 96 payout.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Commerzbank sees steady 96 payout.

text.p: Commerzbank AG, Germany's third largest commercial bank, plans to keep its dividend unchanged this year to boost reserves, chief executive Martin Kohlhaussen said in a newspaper interview published on Monday.
Operating profit would show "good double-digit" percentage growth in the first nine months of 1996, he said.
"We will significantly increase the substance of the bank from this year's earnings, that also benefits the shareholder," Kohlhaussen told Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.

Commerzbank paid a 13.50 mark ($8.86) dividend per 50-mark share on 1995 results after paying 12 marks plus a bonus of 1.50 marks for 1994. The bank has since reduced the nominal value of its shares to five marks in line with other major German companies.
The bank publishes nine-month results at a news conference on November 5. Analysts on average expect an operating profit after risk provisions of 1.8 billion marks.

That would be a year-on-year rise of 47.5 percent -- unchanged from the 47.6 percent growth reported at the half-year stage and well above the earnings rises posted last week by rivals Deutsche Bank AG and Bayerische Vereinsbank AG .
In the interview, Kohlhaussen reiterated that plans to expand its investment banking business, particularly in the area of international equities, through internal growth rather than acquisitions.

But he added he was not against the idea of an acquisition in the U.S. in the field of asset management provided it was a good firm with a solid customer base rather than one that had expanded just because of the stock market rally.
Commerzbank last year bought British asset management firm Jupiter Tyndall and also tried to acquire British stockbroker Smith New Court but lost out to rival bidder Merrill Lynch.
Kohlhaussen said Commerzbank was already a leading player in mark-denominated bond issuance and planned to strengthen its position in non-mark issues.
It was hiring new staff to boost its equities business but, unlike other German banks, was refraining from taking on entire teams, Kohlhaussen said.

"We don't hire whole teams because they then move on to other banks as teams," Kohlhaussen said. Commerzbank last month lost five bond salesman who defected to rival Deutsche Bank AG in London and Frankfurt.
Referring to Commerzbank's domestic retail business, Kohlhaussen said the bank was rationalising by merging branches at a rate of about 20 per year.
Kohlhaussen also said that Commerzbank regarded Frankfurt as its centre of competence, with strong bases in London, New York and Singapore.
